name: Oguchi disease
aliases: congenital stationary night blindness with Mizuo-Nakamura phenomenon

clinicalPearls: Rare autosomal recessive form of congenital stationary night blindness caused by mutations in SAG (arrestin) or GRK1 (rhodopsin kinase), genes needed to deactivate rhodopsin after light exposure
The pathognomonic sign is the Mizuo-Nakamura phenomenon: a golden-yellow or metallic sheen of the fundus in the light-adapted state that reverts to a normal colour after prolonged dark adaptation
Patients report lifelong, non-progressive night blindness with normal daytime acuity and colour vision
Dark adaptometry shows a characteristic profile in which rod sensitivity recovers only after a very prolonged period of dark adaptation
The electroretinogram typically shows an absent or markedly reduced rod b-wave under standard conditions, which can partially recover after extended dark adaptation
It should be distinguished from progressive rod-cone dystrophies, as Oguchi disease is stationary with preserved acuity
Management is supportive with reassurance about the stationary course, advice regarding night vision, and genetic counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Oguchi disease arises from recessive mutations in SAG (S-antigen/arrestin) or GRK1 (rhodopsin kinase), proteins that normally quench activated rhodopsin so that rods can recover after light exposure. Defective deactivation leaves rods persistently desensitised following illumination, producing profound but non-progressive night blindness and abnormally slow dark adaptation. The abnormal state of the rod photoreceptors and their outer segments underlies the Mizuo-Nakamura phenomenon, in which the light-adapted retina takes on a golden sheen that disappears after prolonged darkness.
additionalDifferentials: Other forms of congenital stationary night blindness
Retinitis pigmentosa and progressive rod-cone dystrophies
additionalInvestigations: Fundus examination in light- and dark-adapted states to demonstrate the Mizuo-Nakamura phenomenon
Prolonged dark adaptometry showing delayed rod recovery
Full-field electroretinography before and after extended dark adaptation
Fundus autofluorescence and optical coherence tomography to exclude degeneration
Molecular genetic testing for SAG and GRK1 mutations
Visual field testing to confirm preservation
redFlags: Documented progression of field loss or acuity decline, which is inconsistent with the diagnosis and suggests a degenerative disorder
Pigmentary retinopathy or bone-spicule change indicating retinitis pigmentosa instead
Onset of night blindness in adulthood pointing to an acquired cause
Affected siblings warranting screening given recessive inheritance
reference.prognosis: The condition is stationary and non-progressive; daytime vision remains normal throughout life and only night vision is impaired, so the overall visual prognosis is good.
pitfalls: Overlooking the Mizuo-Nakamura phenomenon by examining the fundus only in the light-adapted state
Misdiagnosing the disorder as progressive retinitis pigmentosa
Interpreting the reduced rod electroretinogram without repeating it after prolonged dark adaptation
Confusing it with fundus albipunctatus, which shows white dots and a different mechanism
management: No specific therapy exists and none is required for the retinal defect, as the condition is stationary with preserved daytime vision; reassurance is central
Counsel on lifelong non-progressive night blindness and slow dark adaptation, with practical adaptation for low-light environments and driving safety
Confirm and document the diagnosis through the Mizuo-Nakamura phenomenon, dark adaptometry and electroretinography, distinguishing it from progressive rod-cone dystrophies
Periodic ophthalmological review with optical coherence tomography and fundus autofluorescence to confirm stability and exclude co-existing degeneration
Molecular confirmation of the SAG or GRK1 mutation
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder, including carrier and family testing
